+ import { boardOf, cleanWorkCard, readWork } from '../src/shared/tickets'
+ import { stepTodos } from '../src/runner/providers/detail'
+ 
+ let clock = 0
+ 
+ const todoStep = (todos: StepTodo[]): AgentStep => ({
+   id: `t${++clock}`,
+   ts: clock,
+   kind: 'tool',
+   name: 'TodoWrite',
+   status: 'done',
+   todos
+ })
+ 
+ const textStep = (text: string): AgentStep => ({
+   id: `b${++clock}`,
+   ts: clock,
+   kind: 'text',
+   status: 'done',
+   text
+ })
+ 
+ const editStep = (...paths: string[]): AgentStep => ({
+   id: `e${++clock}`,
+   ts: clock,
+   kind: 'tool',
+   name: 'Edit',
+   status: 'done',
+   files: paths.map(path => ({ path, added: 1, removed: 0 }))
+ })
+ 
+ const card = (body: object): string => ['```work', JSON.stringify(body), '```'].join('\n')
+ 
+ describe('the list every CLI keeps', () => {
+   it('reads the three states however a provider spells them', () => {
+     expect(stepTodos({ todos: [{ content: 'Draw the rows', status: 'in_progress' }] })).toEqual([
+       { text: 'Draw the rows', status: 'doing' }
+     ])
+     expect(stepTodos({ plan: [{ step: 'Ship it', status: 'completed' }] })).toEqual([
+       { text: 'Ship it', status: 'done' }
+     ])
+     expect(stepTodos({ items: [{ text: 'Ship it', completed: true }] })).toEqual([{ text: 'Ship it', status: 'done' }])
+     expect(stepTodos({ todos: [{ content: 'Later', status: 'pending' }] })).toEqual([
+       { text: 'Later', status: 'todo' }
+     ])
+   })
+ 
+   it('is nothing rather than an empty list when there is none', () => {
+     expect(stepTodos({ command: 'yarn test' })).toBeUndefined()
+     expect(stepTodos({ todos: [] })).toBeUndefined()
+     expect(stepTodos(undefined)).toBeUndefined()
+   })
+ })
+ 
+ describe('a card', () => {
+   it('comes back as null with nothing on it', () => {
+     expect(cleanWorkCard({ kind: 'question' })).toBeNull()
+     expect(cleanWorkCard({ kind: 'decision', text: '  ' })).toBeNull()
+     expect(cleanWorkCard({ kind: 'nonsense', text: 'hi' })).toBeNull()
+     expect(cleanWorkCard('question')).toBeNull()
+   })
+ 
+   it('is taken out of what is read', () => {
+     const written = ['Starting on the sync loop.', card({ kind: 'decision', text: 'Kept the local copy' }), 'Done.'].join(
+       '\n'

+     expect(cards).toEqual([{ kind: 'decision', text: 'Kept the local copy' }])

+ 
+   it('leaves a broken one out rather than showing it', () => {
+     const { text, cards } = readWork(['Working.', '```work', '{not json', '```'].join('\n'))

+ 
+ describe('the board', () => {
+   it('is the columns the agent already keeps', () => {

+     const board = boardOf([
+       todoStep([
+         { text: 'Draw the panel', status: 'doing' },
+         { text: 'Write the test', status: 'todo' }

+       todoStep([{ text: 'Draw the panel', status: 'doing' }])

+

+     const steps = [
+       todoStep([{ text: 'Draw the panel', status: 'doing' }]),

+       todoStep([{ text: 'Draw the panel', status: 'done' }])

+     expect(boardOf(steps)[('tickets' as const)][0].review).toBe('The panel reads off the steps now')
+     expect(boardOf([...steps, todoStep([{ text: 'Draw the panel', status: 'doing' }])]).tickets[0].column).toBe('doing')

+ 
+   it('moves a review to done for whoever has looked at it, and nobody else', () => {

+       textStep(card({ kind: 'review', note: 'Have a look' }))

+     expect(boardOf(steps).tickets[0].column).toBe('review')
+   })
+ 
+   it('says what answering a question late would cost', () => {
+     const board = boardOf([
+       todoStep([{ text: 'Draw the panel', status: 'doing' }]),
+       textStep(card({ kind: 'question', ask: 'Columns or sections?', assumed: 'sections', options: ['columns', 'sections'] })),
+       editStep('a.ts', 'b.ts'),
+       editStep('b.ts', 'c.ts')

+     expect(board.questions).toHaveLength(1)

+     expect(board.questions[0].ticket).toBe('Draw the panel')
+     expect(board.questions[0].options).toEqual(['columns', 'sections'])

step.text: I found the Toggle component, so let me examine it along with the model definitions at the top of claude.ts. Now I'm thinking through where to place the token usage and cost display settings — Appearance seems like the right home since these are display preferences rather than functional settings, even though the page is currently focused on theme. Creating a separate tab just for two checkboxes would be overkill.

Helpers are in. 94 tests across 11 suites pass, `yarn tsc --noEmit` is clean for everything I touched, and `yarn build` builds.

## What it is

An agent splits work off mid-run and keeps going. It makes a helper up as it needs one, a short name and the whole of the piece, so the work decides how it's divided rather than a list somebody wrote last week. One curl line in the preamble, so every provider gets it at once.

**The parent never blocks.** It sends out, gets an id back, carries on. When a helper finishes the host pushes the answer into whatever the parent is doing: into the live turn where the agent is steerable, as a turn of its own where it isn't. Three finishing in a breath are one interruption, not three.

**The handoff isn't a chat message.** `silent` rides on the steer and the queued prompt, so nobody scrolls past a helper's raw answer pasted in as though it had been said. The chip is the record, and it opens onto the whole thing.

**The chips are truth.** Each reads its own thread's state and latest step, so the row reports whether or not the agent ever mentions it. Only `RunStatus` spins; a working chip lights its mark and pulses. Four spawned in one breath fold into one line.

**A helper opens in the side panel** as an ordinary thread: steps, thinking, diffs, files changed, cancel, and a composer that steers it.

## The mark

`cover-sheet-marks.png` from `yarn covers`, every mark at 18, 28 and 64 on both surfaces. Same shader and palette as the music covers, seen through a shape seeded per run: rosettes of 3 to 8 lobes, plus discs, hexagons and squares so a page of them isn't a page of flowers. A lobed mark takes the live area the way the star does; a disc sits on the circle keyline. `MIN_WAIST` is where a rosette stops being one shape.

## Settings

A **Helpers** page under Crew: a switch and a count, both yours alone. Off means no agent on your machine sends work out *or takes anybody else's*, since it's your tokens and your files. Kept in `localStorage`, said again on every connect.

## What I dropped

The toolbox tile, per your message. And the pre-defined roster went with your second one — no roles, no builder, `subagent.add/edit/remove/run` all gone.

## Two things worth knowing

`src/server` changed, so **nothing works until the host window is restarted** — first thing to check when a spawn comes back 404.

Two agents on one file is the one thing the sync loop can't help with. Half of that is words in the preamble; the other half is the panel listing files changed per helper.

The regex pattern that collapses multiple newlines is working as intended—when a card is removed from between two paragraphs, it leaves a single blank line, which is the correct markdown formatting for a paragraph break. The test expectation was actually wrong about what the output should be.

But I'm reconsidering whether that's the right behavior. If a card was sitting mid-paragraph between two sentences, removing it shouldn't introduce a paragraph break—that changes how the text renders. I think the cleaner approach is to collapse that leftover blank line entirely, so I need to modify the regex to consume the trailing newline after the card fence, which will give me "a
b" instead of "a

b" when a card sits between consecutive lines.

+ // The newline after the closing fence goes with it, or a card lifted out from
+ // between two lines leaves a blank one behind and splits the prose in two.
+ const WORK_FENCE = /^[ \t]*```[ \t]*work[ \t]*\r?\n([\s\S]*?)^[ \t]*```[ \t]*\r?\n?/gim

I'm mapping out how to handle costs across different CLI tools. Claude's API returns the exact cost in the response, so that's straightforward. For the others like Codex, Kimi, and Grok, I'll need to build a pricing lookup table keyed by model since they don't include cost data in the stream.

The approach is to parse full usage metrics (input, output, cache reads/writes) and any reported cost, then use a pricing table in `src/shared/pricing.ts` for models I can confidently price—Claude and OpenAI models. If a model isn't in the table, I'll show nothing rather than guess. Claude's reported cost takes precedence when available.

Since the ask is specifically for cost display plus two toggleable settings (show token usage and show token cost), I should implement this properly rather than cutting corners on the pricing data.

The real tension is between using only what the CLI reports (honest and never stale, but incomplete coverage) versus maintaining a pricing table (comprehensive but risks staleness and inaccuracy). The middle ground is to prefer CLI-reported costs and fall back to a table only for well-known public rates, letting unknown models simply show no cost rather than inventing numbers.

But there's a bigger consideration I'm realizing: most crew agents run on subscription CLIs like Claude Code Max or ChatGPT Plus, where the marginal cost per run is effectively zero for users. I'm realizing that since Claude Code already provides `total_cost_usd` directly in the result, I might not need a pricing table at all—I could just pass that value through and display it. But if I want to support other providers eventually, building an extensible table with Claude's rates (which I'm confident about) and leaving placeholders for the others is the honest approach.

Actually, the key insight is that `total_cost_usd` only arrives at the end of the turn, so it can't power a live status line. The per-message `usage` data with input/cache/output tokens and model ID would let me calculate costs incrementally as the run progresses. So the best design is to estimate costs live from the usage table, then anchor to the authoritative total when it arrives—giving a live-updating estimate that settles to the exact figure.

This is a substantial change across multiple files, so I need to plan the scope carefully: runner, shared, server, protocol, renderer, settings, and tests all need updates. Let me start by defining the pricing module...

Writing pricing module... I'll use 1.25× as the default cache write multiplier since that matches the documented TTL, and the live estimate being slightly off is acceptable anyway since the actual cost gets reported at turn end. Rather than storing four numbers per model, I'll just store input and output rates, then derive the cache multipliers from those—it's cleaner and stays in sync with the documented values. Now I need to figure out where to put the `TokenUsage` type, probably in pricing.ts and re-export it from there.

`LiveRun` will get a `cost` field, and in the provider types I'm defining a `ParsedUsage` interface that holds the model name, token counts, cache metrics, and an optional cost field that the CLI can populate when it reports one. Then `ParsedOutput` will reference this usage object.

I'm realizing I can derive the token count from the usage data itself rather than storing it separately — providers would emit usage information, and the CLI can extract both the token count and cost from that single source. This means updating all the places where providers currently push `{ tokens }` to push `usage` instead, which is cleaner and removes duplication. I need to check where `ParsedOutput.tokens` is actually used in the codebase and tests to make sure this refactor won't break anything.

For accumulating usage in the CLI, the challenge is that Claude sends usage data per API call on each assistant message — currently I'm taking the max of token counts, but for cost I need to sum across all calls. For cost calculation, I need to avoid double-counting by keeping separate tracking: a running sum of per-message usage for the live estimate, and a final authoritative value from the result message or CLI override.

I'm setting up the data structure in cli.ts to accumulate individual usage entries marked as non-total, while separately storing whichever entry is marked as the authoritative total, then reporting the final value with the live estimate as a fallback. Defining the usage interface... With `--include-partial-messages`, Claude Code emits both partial stream events and then a final complete `assistant` message with usage data, so the parser correctly captures one usage per API call. Summing the outputs is the right approach, and since the result message provides the cumulative total anyway, any summing errors get corrected at the end. The token count only ever grows with this method, which is consistent with the current behavior, though switching from "max single message output" to "sum of all outputs" does represent a behavioral change worth considering.

Now I'm mapping out the remaining implementation: adding `cost` to the `agent.tokens` protocol in both directions, storing cost on the live run in the session, adding a costs map alongside the tokens map in the renderer's store, displaying cost in RunStatus and the chat thread status, and creating a new preferences file to hold `showTokens` and `showCost` toggles in localStorage with the same structure as the theme settings. I'm leaning toward adding a Section without a title beneath the theme cards to avoid visual separation issues, since Section provides built-in padding. Now I'm deciding on the label text for these toggles—something like "Token usage" and "Token cost" seems clear. The key insight is that people on subscription plans might not realize they're not being charged, so I need a helper line that clarifies this is the theoretical cost at API rates. I'm settling on something straightforward like "What the tokens would cost at standard API rates" for the "Estimated cost" row — it's plain enough for the technically inclined audience while being honest about what the number represents.

For implementation, I'm putting the `formatCost` function alongside `formatTokens` in the time.ts module since that's where the formatting utilities live. The format itself is simple: costs display with two decimal places like `$0.34` or `$1.20`, and anything under a cent shows as `<$0.01`. I need to design the swipe interaction for closing the toast—dragging right past a threshold or with enough velocity should dismiss it, while dragging left resists and doesn't move. I also need to distinguish between a click and a drag by tracking movement and suppressing the click if it exceeds a small threshold, and handle the edge case where the action button might initiate a swipe.

The tricky part is keeping the toast clock paused while dragging—pointer capture will keep events flowing, but if the pointer leaves the stack during a swipe, the clock would resume mid-gesture, so I need to handle that edge case where the pointer travels past the stack boundary. So with pointer capture, the container won't receive pointerleave until capture is released, which means the hold stays active during the drag and resumes correctly when the pointer leaves. For testing, I need to handle the fact that jsdom implements setPointerCapture but it might throw errors, so I should wrap the call defensively to avoid breaking tests.

I'm thinking about extracting the swipe logic into a reusable hook called `useSwipeAway` rather than embedding it directly in the Row component — it keeps the component cleaner and follows the repo's pattern of creating primitives when they're needed, even if only one consumer exists right now.

+ // What a run is worth billed by the token. Agents here run on somebody's own
+ // CLI, usually on a plan that already covers the work, so this is the price of
+ // the tokens rather than a bill anyone is getting.
+ //
+ // A model with no rate comes back as null and nothing is shown. A wrong number
+ // costs more than a missing one, so nothing is ever guessed at: adding a model
+ // is one row here and nowhere else.
+ 
+ export interface TokenUsage {
+   input: number
+   output: number
+   cacheRead: number
+   cacheWrite: number
+ }
+ 
+ export const NO_USAGE: TokenUsage = { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0 }
+ 
+ export function addUsage(a: TokenUsage, b: Partial<TokenUsage>): TokenUsage {
+   return {
+     input: a.input + (b.input ?? 0),
+     output: a.output + (b.output ?? 0),
+     cacheRead: a.cacheRead + (b.cacheRead ?? 0),
+     cacheWrite: a.cacheWrite + (b.cacheWrite ?? 0)
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ // Reading a prefix that is already cached is a tenth of the input rate and
+ // writing one is a quarter more, so a row only has to carry the two rates a
+ // model is sold at.
+ const CACHE_READ = 0.1
+ const CACHE_WRITE = 1.25
+ 
+ // Dollars per million tokens, in and out.
+ const RATES: Record<string, [number, number]> = {
+   'claude-fable-5': [10, 50],
+   'claude-mythos-5': [10, 50],
+   'claude-opus-5': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-8': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-7': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-6': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-5': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-1': [15, 75],
+   'claude-opus-4': [15, 75],
+   'claude-sonnet-5': [3, 15],
+   'claude-sonnet-4-6': [3, 15],
+   'claude-sonnet-4-5': [3, 15],
+   'claude-sonnet-4': [3, 15],
+   'claude-haiku-4-5': [1, 5]
+ }
+ 
+ // A CLI names the model it really used, dated build and all, so a row is a
+ // prefix and the longest one wins: `claude-opus-4-5-20251101` is priced by
+ // `claude-opus-4-5` rather than by `claude-opus-4`.
+ const KEYS = Object.keys(RATES).sort((a, b) => b.length - a.length)
+ 
+ export function rateOf(model: string): [number, number] | null {
+   const key = KEYS.find(name => model.startsWith(name))
+   return key ? RATES[key] : null
+ }
+ 
+ export function priceOf(model: string, usage: TokenUsage): number | null {
+   const rate = rateOf(model.trim())
+   if (!rate) return null
+   const [input, output] = rate
+   const dollars =
+     usage.input * input +
+     usage.output * output +
+     usage.cacheRead * input * CACHE_READ +
+     usage.cacheWrite * input * CACHE_WRITE
+   return dollars / 1_000_000
+ }
+

Jamel's looking for a single ticket icon instead of the board layout. I'm picturing a classic cinema ticket shape—a wide rounded rectangle with semicircular notches cut into both sides at the middle, maybe with a dashed line running through the center for that perforation detail. It fits the design system's style: outlined, geometric, with generous curves and just enough character.

Now I'm working out the dimensions and geometry. A ticket should be wider than it is tall, so I'm using a 19 × 15.2 unit box with 2.25 radius corners to match the crew's proportional guidelines. The notches are semicircles with about a 2-unit radius biting inward from the left and right edges at the vertical center. Adding a short vertical line as a stub perforation completes the mark—two simple elements that read unmistakably as a ticket.

I'm constructing the SVG path now, starting from the top-left corner and moving clockwise around the shape, with special attention to how the notches curve inward... left). By symmetry, the left notch with sweep=0 should also bulge inward (to the right), which is what we want. ✓ The corner arcs use sweep=1 since they're clockwise on screen. ✓ Now I need to figure out what comes between the two notches—whether there's a stub line connecting them or something else.

Looking at how ticket icons typically work: Heroicons has notches on top and bottom with a vertical perforation between them, while the version I'm building has notches on the left and right edges at the vertical middle. That would mean a horizontal perforation across the center, which is an unusual way to tear a ticket. The more standard silhouette everyone recognizes is notches on left and right at the middle height, which matches what I'm going for. I'm going in circles on how to add visual detail without cluttering the icon. A short horizontal line inside the left portion could suggest text on the ticket, but it'll disappear at 16px. The core shape—outline with side notches—is already strong enough to read as a ticket, so maybe I don't need extra marks at all.

Actually, reconsidering the orientation: if I place notches on the left and right edges at mid-height, the tear line runs horizontally between them, splitting the ticket top and bottom. That works for cinema tickets held vertically. But most ticket icons are wider with the perforation running vertically instead, notches on top and bottom—that gives me a stub on the right side, which adds character and is more recognizable.

So I'll go with a wide ticket: notches positioned on the top and bottom edges, a vertical tear line connecting them down the middle, creating that distinctive stub on the right. Now I need to set up the coordinates. the floating line reads as disconnected from the ticket shape itself. The real issue is that at 16px the notches become nearly invisible—a 1.3px radius is too subtle. I should increase the notch radius to 2.75 to make them visible at small sizes, or try a different approach: a taller, narrower ticket oriented vertically with larger side notches at mid-height that would read clearly even when scaled down. But that breaks the conventional wide ticket format, so I'm leaning toward keeping the wide shape and just making those notches more pronounced. Computing the SVG path... Closing the path and verifying the math checks out — the coordinates land on quarter units, though I need to adjust the top and bottom values slightly to keep everything aligned to quarters. Setting T to 4.5 and B to 19.5 gives me a height of 15, and the width works out to roughly 19, which keeps the proportions within acceptable tolerance. I need to check how the icon renders against the audit's ink metrics, then run the test suite. I'm also renaming BoardGlyph to TicketGlyph throughout the codebase since the icon represents a ticket, not a board.

+ import type { ParsedUsage } from './types'
+ 
+ // Every CLI names the same four numbers differently, and they disagree about
+ // one of them: the part of the input that came off a cache is counted beside
+ // the input by Anthropic and inside it by OpenAI. Read the wrong way round, a
+ // long cached prefix is charged twice at full rate, so which shape a message is
+ // in has to be decided rather than guessed.
+ 
+ const count = (value: unknown): number | undefined =>
+   typeof value === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value) ? value : undefined
+ 
+ export function usageFrom(usage: unknown, model?: unknown): ParsedUsage | null {
+   if (!usage || typeof usage !== 'object') return null
+   const raw = usage as Record<string, any>
+   const name = typeof model === 'string' && model.trim() ? model : undefined
+   const output = count(raw.output_tokens) ?? count(raw.completion_tokens)
+ 
+   const read = count(raw.cache_read_input_tokens)
+   const written = count(raw.cache_creation_input_tokens)
+   if (read !== undefined || written !== undefined) {
+     return { model: name, input: count(raw.input_tokens), output, cacheRead: read, cacheWrite: written }
+   }
+ 
+   const input = count(raw.input_tokens) ?? count(raw.prompt_tokens)
+   const cached = count(raw.cached_input_tokens) ?? count(raw.prompt_tokens_details?.cached_tokens)
+   if (cached !== undefined && input !== undefined) {
+     return { model: name, input: Math.max(0, input - cached), output, cacheRead: cached }
+   }
+   if (input === undefined && output === undefined) return null
+   return { model: name, input, output }
+ }
+

Now I'm designing the `useSwipeAway` hook with constants for detecting swipe gestures—a small slop threshold to distinguish swipes from presses, a distance threshold for when the swipe registers as "away," and a flick velocity to let quick gestures carry through regardless of distance.

+ import { useRef, useState, type CSSProperties, type PointerEvent } from 'react'
+ 
+ // Pushing something out of the way to the right. It follows the pointer while it
+ // is held, and on letting go it either carries on and goes or springs back to
+ // where it was. A gesture that travelled is not a press, so whatever it was
+ // dragged from asks `moved` before it treats the click as one.
+ const SLOP = 6
+ const AWAY = 88
+ const FLICK = 0.45
+ const CLEAR = 40
+ 
+ export interface SwipeAway {
+   props: {
+     style: CSSProperties
+     'data-swiping'?: string
+     onPointerDown: (event: PointerEvent<HTMLElement>) => void
+     onPointerMove: (event: PointerEvent<HTMLElement>) => void
+     onPointerUp: (event: PointerEvent<HTMLElement>) => void
+     onPointerCancel: (event: PointerEvent<HTMLElement>) => void
+   }
+   moved: () => boolean
+ }
+ 
+ interface Grab {
+   from: number
+   x: number
+   at: number
+   speed: number
+ }
+ 
+ export function useSwipeAway(onAway: () => void): SwipeAway {
+   const [x, setX] = useState(0)
+   const [swiping, setSwiping] = useState(false)
+   const grab = useRef<Grab | null>(null)
+   const moved = useRef(false)
+   const gone = useRef(false)
+ 
+   // Far enough, or fast enough however far it got. A flick is how somebody
+   // brushes one of these aside, and it lands well short of the distance.
+   const end = (event: PointerEvent<HTMLElement>): void => {
+     const held = grab.current
+     if (!held) return
+     grab.current = null
+     setSwiping(false)
+     event.currentTarget.releasePointerCapture?.(event.pointerId)
+     if (held.x < AWAY && !(held.x > SLOP && held.speed > FLICK)) return setX(0)
+     gone.current = true
+     setX(held.x + event.currentTarget.offsetWidth + CLEAR)
+     onAway()
+   }
+ 
+   return {
+     moved: () => moved.current,
+     props: {
+       style: {
+         transform: `translateX(${x}px)`,
+         opacity: gone.current ? 0 : 1 - Math.min(x / (AWAY * 3), 0.5)
+       },
+       'data-swiping': swiping ? '' : undefined,
+       onPointerDown: event => {
+         if (event.button !== 0) return
+         moved.current = false
+         grab.current = { from: event.clientX, x: 0, at: performance.now(), speed: 0 }
+         setSwiping(true)
+         event.currentTarget.setPointerCapture?.(event.pointerId)
+       },
+       onPointerMove: event => {
+         const held = grab.current
+         if (!held) return
+         const travelled = event.clientX - held.from
+         if (!moved.current && Math.abs(travelled) < SLOP) return
+         moved.current = true
+         // It only goes one way, so pulling the other way holds it where it is
+         // rather than dragging it under whatever it stands beside.
+         const next = Math.max(0, travelled)

That is the whole of the flow columns, with no brief and nothing for a model to cooperate with.
- The one line a step says about a list is still narrated, "Drawing the rows", because that is what a live step reads like. A ticket is the same item named rather than narrated, "Draw the rows", which is why `activeForm` wins in one place and nowhere else.
- A question never stops the work. The agent raises it, answers it for itself, and carries on, and the row says what it assumed. Answering costs one press, and what answering late would cost is on the row as the number of files that have changed since, so interrupting is a number rather than a feeling.
- A decision hangs off whatever ticket was being worked on when it was written, which is read off the list rather than matched by anything the model has to get right. One written before there was a list waits for the first ticket that is picked up.
- In review is the column that pays for the rest. Everything else is already readable in the thread, and this is the agent saying a slice is finished. Both ways out are real messages: a sentence goes back as a steer aimed at that slice, and picking the ticket up again is what the board reads as the way out of review.

- `TICKET_INSTRUCTIONS` is added to every prompt in the thread the way plan mode and voice add theirs, and nothing about it is ever a message. Only Claude takes a steer mid-run, so anywhere else an answer joins the queue.

I'm seeing why the short swipe triggered the close—24 pixels is less than the AWAY threshold of 88, so it shouldn't have fired the flick logic. But the flick condition checks if `held.x > SLOP && held.speed > FLICK`, and with performance.now potentially faked at 0, the time delta becomes false, keeping speed at 0, which means the flick shouldn't fire either. If performance.now isn't faked though, the real time between pointerdown and pointermove could be under 1ms, giving a tiny time delta like 0.05ms that might still register as a valid speed calculation.

The core issue is that 24 pixels in 0.05ms yields a speed of 480 px/ms, which absolutely triggers the flick threshold—but that's physically impossible in a real browser. A genuine 24-pixel movement in one frame (16ms) would be 1.5 px/ms, which is still above the 0.45 flick threshold and would legitimately close the toast. The flick logic itself is sound, but it's extremely sensitive to how time deltas are measured in tests.

I need to make this more robust by either ignoring samples with very small time deltas (below something like 8ms) or accumulating them, and keeping a trailing window of samples to smooth out the speed calculation rather than relying on single-event precision.

The approach I'm settling on: track a mark with position and timestamp, only updating it when at least 30ms has elapsed since the last mark. This ensures speed reflects meaningful travel distance over a reasonable time window. On pointer release, I compute speed from the last mark to the final position, but I need to be careful about the tail of the gesture—the release often comes immediately after the last move event, which would again create a tiny dt and inflated speed.

The safest solution is to use only the speed computed during the last completed sample window, which is what most implementations do with velocity decay. This fixes both test failures: the quick 24px swipe now correctly springs back since it doesn't accumulate enough samples to register as a flick, and the 140px swipe still triggers the action as intended.

Writing the pointer event handlers... Restructuring the hook with this approach. The speed naturally decays to zero if the finger stops moving before release, since a stationary sample gives zero velocity. And with deterministic timing in tests, this works cleanly whether performance.now() is mocked or real.

The Toaster's container is fixed-positioned. Its child card is static with a transform. When the card's transform pushes it past the viewport edge, the card's overflow contributes to the fixed element's scrollable overflow. A fixed element with overflow visible (the default) propagates that overflow up to the viewport. Chrome does create scrollbars for overflowing content inside fixed elements—this is a known behavior. So the scrollbar appears because the fixed container's child overflows.

`body { overflow: hidden }` (or `overflow-x: clip`) will prevent the viewport from scrolling, which stops the scrollbar. Since the app never scrolls the window anyway, this is safe.

Swipe is in. A toast now follows the pointer to the right and either carries on out or springs back.

**How it behaves**
- Past 88px it goes, or a flick takes it however far it got. Under that it springs back.
- Pulling left holds it where it stands rather than dragging it under the row beside it.
- A gesture is never a press as well: swiping does not fire the row's own way out, and does not press an Undo sitting on it.
- Text selection is off on the card, so a drag across the words is the swipe and nothing else.

**Where it lives**
- `src/renderer/src/components/useSwipeAway.ts` is a primitive rather than something wired into the one caller. Speed is read over a 30ms window, because two pointer events can land in the same fraction of a millisecond and a few pixels over nearly no time reads as a flick no hand ever made.
- `Toaster.tsx` spreads it onto the card and asks `moved()` before treating a click as a press.
- `styles.css`: the card carries the transition that springs it back, and drops it while the pointer is on it so it is where the hand is on the frame it is there.

**The scrollbar**: the stack is portaled to the body, which `#root`'s clip does not cover, so a card pushed past the right edge grew the window. The window never scrolls, so `body` clips now. That also covers the ordinary gesture, not just the flight, since the card starts 24px from the edge and crosses it almost immediately.

The issue is that `prefs.ts` initializes its module state by reading localStorage immediately on load, before tests can stub it out. Since each test stubs localStorage independently, the initial read happens before the stub is in place, causing state to leak between tests. I need to either reset the preferences between tests or expose a function that re-reads from the stubbed localStorage.

The cleanest approach is to make the cache check the raw storage value on each read—if the raw string has changed, re-parse it. This way, when a test stubs localStorage, the next call to `prefs()` will detect the change and update the cached state accordingly.

In Node environments without localStorage, `setPref` becomes a no-op while `prefs()` always returns the defaults, which is fine since the renderer always has storage available. The logic handles the initial `null` state correctly—when storage is empty, `raw` stays `null` and matches the initial `seen` value, so it returns defaults without attempting to parse. subject: the dictation rules and their tests

text:
Write two new files in the crew repo and nothing else. Do not touch any other file. Read AGENTS.md first and follow it: no code comments unless a rule needs explaining in the project's own voice, no em dashes anywhere, TypeScript, small files, SOLID, DRY.

This is for a feature called Scribe: hold a hotkey, talk, and what you said is written into whatever app you are in. Whisper transcribes it. Your job is the pass that turns what whisper heard into what a person meant to write.

FILE 1: src/shared/scribeTidy.ts. Pure, no imports of anything outside src/shared, no dependencies, no DOM, no node APIs. It must export exactly this API and it must typecheck under the repo tsconfig:

  export interface ScribeChunk { text: string; start: number; end: number }
  export interface TidyRules { fillers: boolean; stutters: boolean; corrections: boolean; marks: boolean; words: Array<{ from: string; to: string }> }
  export const TIDY_RULES: TidyRules  (all four booleans true, words empty)
  export function tidy(chunks: readonly ScribeChunk[], rules?: TidyRules): string

start and end are SECONDS, the way whisper's return_timestamps gives them. A chunk is roughly a word or a short run of words. The gap between one chunk's end and the next one's start is real signal and is half of what you are working with. Chunks can arrive with end === start, or with a null-ish 0, so never divide by a duration without guarding it.

tidy() does, in an order you decide and can defend:

1. FILLERS (rules.fillers). Drop um, uh, uhh, er, erm, ah, mm, mmm, hmm, huh as standalone words wherever they appear. Then drop like, you know, I mean, sort of, kind of, basically, literally, right ONLY where they stand alone as an aside, never inside real use. "I mean it" keeps its words. "sort of blue" keeps its words. "it was, like, huge" loses the like. Be conservative: when in doubt keep the word. A dropped filler must not leave a double space or a stranded comma.

2. STUTTERS (rules.stutters). An immediately repeated word collapses to one: "the the file" to "the file", "I I think" to "I think". Case-insensitive on the compare, and the one that survives is the first one's casing unless the second is capitalized at a sentence start. Also collapse a false start where a short run of words is immediately said again: "I want, I want to ship" leaves "I want to ship", "we should we should go" leaves "we should go". Cap the run you look back over so this stays linear, three or four words is plenty. Never collapse a genuine repetition like "very very good" or "had had" if you can tell them apart cheaply; if you cannot, prefer collapsing, because a doubled word is the commoner mistake.

3. SELF-CORRECTION (rules.corrections). These phrases cut back to the start of the current sentence and take themselves with them: scratch that, strike that, delete that, forget that, no wait, wait no, actually no, sorry no, I mean no. So "let's use redis, scratch that, let's use postgres" becomes "Let's use postgres." And "scratch all that", "scratch everything", "delete all that", "start over" take the WHOLE dictation so far, leaving only what follows. A sentence boundary for this purpose is a mark already in the text or a long gap you decided was one.

4. MARKS (rules.marks). Keep every mark whisper emitted. Where it emitted none, place them from the gaps: a gap of about 0.7s or more between two chunks closes a sentence with a full stop, a gap of about 0.35s takes a comma if the run before it reads like a clause rather than one or two words. Never put a comma directly before an existing mark, never double a mark, and never end on a comma: a trailing comma becomes a full stop. A sentence that runs past about 30 words with no mark in it takes one at the best gap it has. If the whole dictation ends with no mark, give it a full stop, unless it ends in ? or !.

5. CAPITALS. Every sentence opens on a capital. The standalone word i becomes I, and i'm i'll i've i'd follow. One space after a mark, none before it, and no space before an apostrophe's contraction.

6. DICTIONARY (rules.words). Whole-word, case-insensitive replacements applied to the words: {from: "claude", to: "Claude"} makes every standalone claude read Claude. It must not match inside a longer word. Apply these late, and whatever casing the replacement carries is what lands.

Nothing spoken is ever read as a mark. "period", "comma", "new line" are ordinary words and stay as words. "the period after the war" must come through untouched. That is deliberate and is the one thing the person asking for this was firm about.

Empty input gives an empty string. A dictation that is entirely fillers gives an empty string, not a lone full stop.

FILE 2: tests/scribe-tidy.test.ts. Vitest, importing from ../src/shared/scribeTidy. Look at an existing suite in tests/ first to match the house style. Write a real table of spoken-in to written-out, with realistic timestamps in the fixtures so the gap rules are actually exercised rather than trivially satisfied. Cover at minimum: the filler examples above, both stutter shapes, both correction scopes, a 0.9s gap becoming a full stop, a 0.4s gap becoming a comma, "I mean it" untouched, "sort of blue" untouched, "the period after the war" untouched, the standalone i capitalized, a dictionary replacement landing and not matching inside a longer word, each rule switched off leaving its input alone, and empty input. Include a few longer, realistic dictations of the kind somebody would actually speak into a chat box, so the rules are tested together rather than only one at a time.

When you are done run: yarn tsc --noEmit  and  yarn test tests/scribe-tidy.test.ts  and make both pass. Do not run the whole test suite. Do not run yarn dev. Report back the exact exported API you settled on and anything you decided differently from the above and why.

text:
Draw one new icon for the crew app and change nothing else in the repo.

Use the skill at .claude/skills/crew-icons: read it in full and follow it exactly. Also read the Design section of AGENTS.md, particularly the paragraph about the 24 grid, the round 2 stroke, and the keylines in src/renderer/src/icons/keylines.ts.

The icon is called ScribeGlyph and it goes in src/renderer/src/icons/media.tsx, beside MicGlyph. Whatever the icons barrel does for the rest of that file must work for this one too, so that `import { ScribeGlyph } from src/renderer/src/icons` resolves. If the barrel re-exports explicitly, add it there; that is the only other file you may touch.

What it is for: a new feature called Scribe. You hold a hotkey, you talk, and what you said is written down into whatever app you are in. It is dictation. The mark stands on a toolbox tile and in the settings rail, at 16 to 20 across.

It must NOT be a microphone. MicGlyph is already in that file and belongs to Voice, which is a different feature, and the two stand near each other. So the mark has to say writing-from-speech some other way. A pen or a nib is the obvious direction and is a fine answer if it is drawn well and reads at 16. Consider also a nib with a line of writing under it, or a stroke of writing that resolves into a mark. Draw two or three candidates, look at them honestly at the real size, and ship the one that is legible smallest, not the one that is cleverest. Whatever you pick must be told apart at 16 from every mark already in src/renderer/src/icons, especially the page, the pencil, the sparkle and the mic.

The stroke is round 2 on a 24 grid, and the mark is measured against its family rather than fitted to its box: a diagonal takes the 19.5 live area, a square sits on 17, a circle on 18.5.

Run `yarn icons` to draw the sheet and read what it measures. Look at the sheet it produces rather than only its numbers. Run `yarn test tests/icons.test.ts` and make it pass. Run `yarn tsc --noEmit`. Do not run the whole test suite and do not run yarn dev.

Report back what you drew, what you rejected and why, and the numbers yarn icons printed for it against its family.

I'm working through the design for a Scribe glyph—something that represents voice dictation and needs to be visually distinct from other glyphs like page, pencil, spark, and microphone icons at small sizes. A fountain pen nib is one candidate, though at 16 pixels it would read more as a triangle shape.

I'm also considering a pen with a writing line underneath it to convey the writing action, though that risks being too similar to the pencil glyph. A quill or feather would be classically appropriate for a scribe but requires too much detail at this scale. Another approach is a waveform that transitions into a written line—showing speech becoming text—but the vertical bars might look like hatching rather than sound waves. A simpler option is just a cursive scrawl on a baseline to represent handwriting directly.

The strongest candidate seems to be a nib pointed downward with a stroke trailing behind it, which captures the essence of writing happening. A caret with writing could work too, though that reads more like a text field. For the nib specifically, the challenge is making it legible at 16 pixels—I need the characteristic slit down the middle and the rounded vent hole to read as a nib rather than a generic triangle or shield. With a 2-stroke outline, the counter space between the slit and edges would be around 2 pixels, which is tight but potentially workable.

I'm also considering adding a baseline of writing beneath the nib to reinforce the dictation concept, though that risks adding too much detail. A 45-degree angled nib with a short writing line underneath could work, but I need to be careful not to create too much visual similarity with the pencil glyph—if both are long diagonals with points, they'll be hard to distinguish at small sizes. The solution is to keep the nib short and upright rather than extending it as a full-length diagonal pen. the nib angled and short, with the writing stroke it produces running away from it—nib in the upper right, tilted, with a line of writing trailing down and left, like a classic signature icon. I'm thinking through which approach reads best at small sizes, and considering a few concrete candidates to actually sketch out: an upright nib on its own as a full mark, versus a nib paired with a writing stroke.

I'm also exploring a couple other directions—sound waves that resolve into a written baseline, or just a simple nib with a ruled line underneath. Let me render these candidates and see how they look, probably by taking screenshots of the icon sheet that the build process already generates.

Build a temp dir with `index.html`, a `main.tsx` that stubs `useCrew.setState({...})`
and renders the component at a fixed size, and a `probe.css`. **The css must be**

```css
@import "<repo>/src/renderer/src/styles.css";
@source "<repo>/src/renderer/src";
```

**Why:** Tailwind v4 detects content from the vite root. Importing `styles.css`
directly from a probe outside the repo compiles only the classes used in the probe
file itself, so the component renders completely unstyled and looks broken for a
reason that has nothing to do with the component. `@source` points the scan back at
the real tree.

**How to apply:** Put the probe under `node_modules/.<name>/` so nothing lands in
the auto-committing tree, `npx vite build --config <probe>/vite.config.ts`, then an
Electron main that `loadFile`s the built `dist/index.html`, waits ~1s and writes
`capturePage().toPNG()`. Delete the probe afterwards. Same shape as
`scripts/cover-sheet.mjs`, which is the committed version of this trick.

The vite config needs `base: './'`. Without it the built html asks for
`/assets/index.js`, which under `file://` is the disk root, so the page loads,
`did-finish-load` fires, nothing throws, and the capture is a black rectangle.
Check `document.getElementById('root').innerHTML.length` before believing a blank
shot. To see a `:hover` state, `webContents.insertCSS` the state on before capture,
since nothing can hover a headless window.
Related: [[crew-design-system]].

+ const OTHER_KEYS: ScribeKey[] = ['right-ctrl', 'ctrl', 'meta', 'right-option']
+ 
+ const MAC_LABELS: Record<ScribeKey, string> = {
+   fn: 'Fn',
+   'right-option': 'Right Option',
+   'right-ctrl': 'Right Control',
+   ctrl: 'Control',
+   meta: 'Command',
+   none: 'Off'
+ }
+ 
+ const OTHER_LABELS: Record<ScribeKey, string> = {
+   fn: 'Fn',
+   'right-option': 'Right Alt',
+   'right-ctrl': 'Right Ctrl',
+   ctrl: 'Ctrl',
+   meta: 'Windows',
+   none: 'Off'
+ }
+ 
+ const isMac = (platform: string): boolean => platform === 'darwin'
+ 
+ export const keyLabel = (key: ScribeKey, platform: string): string =>
+   (isMac(platform) ? MAC_LABELS : OTHER_LABELS)[key] ?? MAC_LABELS.none
+ 
+ // Fn on a Mac because it is the one key nothing else has a claim on, and Right
+ // Control everywhere else for the same reason. Plain Control is offered because
+ // the rule that any other key cancels the take makes it safe, not because it is
+ // a good first answer.
+ export const defaultKey = (platform: string): ScribeKey => (isMac(platform) ? 'fn' : 'right-ctrl')
+ 
+ export const scribeKeys = (platform: string): ScribeKey[] => (isMac(platform) ? MAC_KEYS : OTHER_KEYS)
+ 
+ // A combination that is registered the ordinary way and stays live whatever the
+ // low level hook is doing. The hook is the good key and this is the one that
+ // cannot go quiet, so there is always a way to dictate.
+ export const fallbackCombo = (platform: string): string =>
+   isMac(platform) ? 'Control+Command+Space' : 'Control+Alt+Space'
+ 
+ export const fallbackLabel = (platform: string): string =>
+   isMac(platform) ? 'Control Command Space' : 'Ctrl Alt Space'
+ 
+ export function defaultSettings(platform: string): ScribeSettings {
+   return {
+     on: false,
+     key: defaultKey(platform),
+     press: 'latch',
+     finish: 'paste',
+     fillers: true,
+     stutters: true,
+     corrections: true,
+     marks: true,
+     ready: false,
+     words: []
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ const bool = (value: unknown, fallback: boolean): boolean =>
+   typeof value === 'boolean' ? value : fallback
+ 
+ const one = <T extends string>(value: unknown, of: readonly T[], fallback: T): T =>
+   typeof value === 'string' && (of as readonly string[]).includes(value) ? (value as T) : fallback
+ 
+ const text = (value: unknown): string => (typeof value === 'string' ? value.trim() : '')
+ 
+ // What arrives is only ever as good as what checks it. These come back off
+ // storage written by an older build, or by hand, so nothing is taken on trust.
+ function cleanWords(input: unknown): ScribeWord[] {
+   if (!Array.isArray(input)) return []
+   const out: ScribeWord[] = []
+   const seen = new Set<string>()
+   for (const row of input) {
+     if (!row || typeof row !== 'object') continue
+     const from = text((row as ScribeWord).from)
+     const to = text((row as ScribeWord).to)
+     const key = from.toLowerCase()
+     if (!from || !to || seen.has(key)) continue
+     seen.add(key)
+     out.push({ from, to })
+     if (out.length === WORD_LIMIT) break
+   }
+   return out
+ }
+ 
+ export function cleanSettings(input: unknown, platform: string): ScribeSettings {
+   const base = defaultSettings(platform)
+   if (!input || typeof input !== 'object') return base
+   const held = input as Partial<ScribeSettings>
+   const keys = [...scribeKeys(platform), 'none' as const]
+   return {
+     on: bool(held.on, base.on),
+     key: one(held.key, keys, base.key),
+     press: one(held.press, ['hold', 'toggle', 'latch'] as const, base.press),
+     finish: one(held.finish, ['paste', 'copy'] as const, base.finish),
+     fillers: bool(held.fillers, base.fillers),
+     stutters: bool(held.stutters, base.stutters),
+     corrections: bool(held.corrections, base.corrections),
+     marks: bool(held.marks, base.marks),
+     ready: bool(held.ready, base.ready),
+     words: cleanWords(held.words)
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ export function rulesOf(settings: ScribeSettings): TidyRules {
+   return {
+     ...TIDY_RULES,
+     fillers: settings.fillers,
+     stutters: settings.stutters,
+     corrections: settings.corrections,
+     marks: settings.marks,
+     words: settings.words
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ export type { ScribeWord, TidyRules }
+

step.text:
So libuiohook doesn't capture the Fn key on macOS at all—there's no event flag or virtual code for it. That means the plan's approach to detecting Fn won't work through this library. I can either fall back to using Right Option as a substitute on Mac like originally planned, or write a custom native addon, but that's beyond scope. There might be a third option worth exploring though.

Actually, I'm checking whether libuiohook at least passes through unmapped keys as `VC_UNDEFINED`, but looking at the modifier handling code, when only Fn changes it doesn't trigger any of the four mask branches, so no event gets emitted at all. That's a dead end. The right move is to make the Mac default Right Option and simply exclude Fn from the available keys on macOS rather than offering something that won't work. But I need to be transparent about this limitation instead of silently dropping it.

I'm updating the type definition to remove `'fn'` entirely from the ScribeKey union, which means adjusting the Mac key list to just right-option, right-ctrl, ctrl, and meta. The settings page will get a note explaining that macOS doesn't expose Fn to applications. And I need to handle the case where old settings might have stored 'fn' as a value, which the fallback logic should already cover since it won't be in the available list anymore.

Now I'm sketching out the state machine for scribe-keys.ts: tracking whether the chosen modifier is held down, when it was pressed, whether the arm callback has fired, if a take is currently latched from a tap, and whether another key was pressed while the modifier was held. The keydown handler needs to detect when the chosen modifier goes down, start an arming timer, and mark the state as spoiled if any other key is pressed—though latched takes shouldn't be cancelled by typing since the user might be dictating into another application. less than ARM_MS but nothing else was pressed, that counts as a deliberate tap of the bare modifier and should latch anyway. So on release, if it wasn't spoiled and we're still holding, we latch regardless of whether we've armed yet.

The logic becomes cleaner: if released before TAP_MS and not spoiled, latch; if released after TAP_MS while armed, finish; if spoiled at any point, cancel. This preserves the no-flash-on-Ctrl+C behavior since Ctrl+C spoils the modifier.

There's a trade-off though: accidentally pressing Right Option briefly could latch and open the mic, but that's the same behavior as Wispr, and the pill has an X to close it anyway.

Now I'm thinking through the different press modes — 'hold' releases always finish or cancel with no latch, 'toggle' acts on release when unspoiled regardless of duration, and 'latch' uses the combined rule I just outlined.

Defining the release handler... → arm, press again → finish. That's the global shortcut behavior: always a toggle, regardless of the `press` setting. For the arming timer, I'll use setTimeout to check if the key's still held and not spoiled after ARM_MS fires. The LONGEST_MS cap belongs in the renderer's store since it owns the audio, but I need the keys object to expose a `stopped()` method so the store can reset the latch when the user clicks the pill's check or X button.

The keys class needs to track when a take ends so the next key press starts fresh rather than trying to finish a dead one. I'm defining the public API with methods to apply settings, signal when a take stops, check if the hook is active, and close the connection. On macOS I'll call the accessibility trust check when arming and return that state so the UI can display it, since libuiohook requires accessibility permissions there.

The uiohook module is CommonJS, so I need to be careful about how I load it in the ESM main process—if the native module fails to load, the whole process crashes. I'll wrap the require in a try/catch and load it lazily instead of at import time. For tests, I need to drive the state machine by hand without the native module, so I'm extracting the pure logic into its own module that tests can use independently.

Writing the state machine module... Defining the state machine logic... Refining the state machine logic...

I'm spotting a bug in toggle mode where pressing when armed would emit 'finish' and set armed to false, but then release() would see armed as false and arm again. I need to track whether a press already completed its action with a consumed flag, so release() knows not to re-arm after the press has already finished.

In latch mode, pressing while latched should emit 'finish' and set consumed to true, so the release does nothing. For the stopped() method, I'm resetting armed and latched to false, and setting consumed based on whether the key is still held down to prevent re-finishing on release.

I'm also making hold mode only arm on tick, so a quick tap does nothing—which is the correct behavior for hold mode, even if it means someone holding for 150ms gets nothing.

Now I need to handle the fallback globalShortcut path separately. I'll add a combo flag to ScribeKeys and call arm/finish directly while keeping the latch's armed state in sync by adding a toggled() method that either finishes and disarms if already armed, or arms and latches if not.
Confirmed by reading libuiohook's source: it never reports Fn on macOS. Noting that and moving to Right Option, as the plan said it would.

+ import { ARM_MS, TAP_MS, type ScribePress } from './scribe'
+ 
+ // What one key does over time. It is numbers and nothing else, the way the games
+ // are: no keyboard, no timer of its own, no electron. Whatever is really
+ // listening feeds it presses and the clock, and it says what should happen.
+ //
+ // Four rules make a bare modifier bearable, and each one is here because without
+ // it the key is unusable. It does not arm until it has been held alone, so
+ // reaching for a shortcut never raises the pill. Any other key drops the take
+ // and lets the shortcut through. A tap latches, so a hold is a hold and a tap is
+ // hands free, which is one rule rather than a mode to pick. And a press while it
+ // is latched is what ends it.
+ 
+ export type LatchWord = 'nothing' | 'arm' | 'finish' | 'cancel'
+ 
+ export class ScribeLatch {
+   private down = false
+   private downAt = 0
+   private spoiled = false
+   private armed = false
+   private latched = false
+   // The press has already done its work, so the release that follows does none.
+   // Without it a toggle ends a take on the way down and opens another on the way
+   // back up, which reads as a key that cannot be turned off.
+   private spent = false
+ 
+   constructor(private press: ScribePress) {}
+ 
+   mode(press: ScribePress): void {
+     this.press = press
+   }
+ 
+   get running(): boolean {
+     return this.armed
+   }
+ 
+   get holding(): boolean {
+     return this.down
+   }
+ 
+   keyDown(at: number): LatchWord {
+     if (this.down) return 'nothing'
+     this.down = true
+     this.downAt = at
+     this.spoiled = false
+     this.spent = false
+     if (this.armed && (this.latched || this.press === 'toggle')) {
+       this.armed = false
+       this.latched = false
+       this.spent = true
+       return 'finish'
+     }
+     return 'nothing'
+   }
+ 
+   // The arming delay, come round. Nothing arms on the way down, so a key that
+   // turned out to be the front of a shortcut never opened a microphone.
+   tick(at: number): LatchWord {
+     if (!this.down || this.spoiled || this.spent || this.armed) return 'nothing'
+     if (this.press === 'toggle') return 'nothing'
+     if (at - this.downAt < ARM_MS) return 'nothing'
+     this.armed = true
+     this.latched = false
+     return 'arm'
+   }
+ 
+   // Anything else pressed while the key is held. This is the whole of what makes
+   // plain Control safe to dictate on.
+   other(): LatchWord {
+     if (!this.down || this.spoiled) return 'nothing'
+     this.spoiled = true
+     if (!this.armed) return 'nothing'
+     this.armed = false
+     this.latched = false
+     return 'cancel'
+   }
+ 
+   keyUp(at: number): LatchWord {
+     if (!this.down) return 'nothing'
+     const held = at - this.downAt
+     const spoiled = this.spoiled || this.spent
+     this.down = false
+     this.spoiled = false
+     this.spent = false
+     if (spoiled) return 'nothing'
+     if (this.press === 'toggle') return this.open(true)
+     if (this.press === 'hold') {
+       if (!this.armed) return 'nothing'
+       this.armed = false
+       this.latched = false
+       return 'finish'
+     }
+     // Let go of inside the tap window it stays on, however far in it was: a tap
+     // quick enough never to have armed is still a tap, and doing nothing with it
+     // reads as a key that only works if you are slow.
+     if (!this.armed) return held < TAP_MS ? this.open(true) : 'nothing'
+     if (this.latched) return 'nothing'
+     if (held < TAP_MS) {
+       this.latched = true
+       return 'nothing'
+     }
+     this.armed = false
+     return 'finish'
+   }
+ 
+   // The combination that is always live, which only ever gets a press. It is a
+   // toggle whatever the key is set to, because a release is never coming.
+   toggled(): LatchWord {
+     if (this.armed) {
+       this.armed = false
+       this.latched = false
+       this.spent = this.down
+       return 'finish'
+     }
+     return this.open(this.down)
+   }
+ 
+   // The take ended some other way: the check on the pill, the X, a failure, or
+   // the cap on how long one may run.
+   stopped(): void {
+     this.armed = false
+     this.latched = false
+     this.spent = this.down
+   }
+ 
+   private open(spend: boolean): LatchWord {
+     this.armed = true
+     this.latched = true
+     this.spent = spend
+     return 'arm'
+   }
+ }

+ import { BrowserWindow, screen } from 'electron'
+ import type { ScribeSettings } from '../shared/scribe'
+ import type { PanelPage } from './tray-panel'
+ import { createScribeOptions } from './window-options'
+ 
+ // The pill, and the window it stands in. Frameless, transparent, above
+ // everything, and never focused: whatever you were typing in has to keep the
+ // caret, or a dictation would land nowhere.
+ 
+ const WIDTH = 216
+ const HEIGHT = 56
+ const MAX_HEIGHT = 140
+ // How far off the bottom of the screen it sits. Low enough to be out of the way
+ // and high enough to clear a dock.
+ const LIFT = 96
+ 
+ export class ScribeWindow {
+   private win: BrowserWindow | null = null
+   private settings: ScribeSettings | null = null
+ 
+   constructor(private readonly page: PanelPage) {}
+ 
+   owns(win: BrowserWindow): boolean {
+     return this.win === win
+   }
+ 
+   // Built and loaded before anyone presses the key, the way the tray panel is,
+   // and for a bigger reason: this window holds whisper, and a model that has to
+   // be fetched at the moment somebody starts talking is a first dictation that
+   // arrives a minute late.
+   warm(): void {
+     this.window()
+   }
+ 
+   show(): void {
+     const win = this.window()
+     this.place()
+     // Never `show`, which would take the focus off the app being dictated into
+     // and land the paste in the wrong place, or nowhere at all.
+     win.showInactive()
+   }
+ 
+   hide(): void {
+     this.win?.hide()
+   }
+ 
+   get showing(): boolean {
+     return this.win?.isVisible() ?? false
+   }
+ 
+   send(channel: string, ...args: unknown[]): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win || win.webContents.isDestroyed()) return
+     win.webContents.send(channel, ...args)
+   }
+ 
+   apply(settings: ScribeSettings): void {
+     this.settings = settings
+     this.send('scribe:settings', settings)
+   }
+ 
+   resize(height: number): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win) return
+     const wanted = Math.round(Math.max(HEIGHT, Math.min(height, MAX_HEIGHT)))
+     if (win.getBounds().height === wanted) return
+     win.setBounds({ ...win.getBounds(), height: wanted })
+     this.place()
+   }
+ 
+   close(): void {
+     this.win?.destroy()
+     this.win = null
+   }
+ 
+   // The screen the pointer is on rather than the primary one, because that is
+   // the screen the app being typed into is almost certainly on.
+   private place(): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win) return
+     const bounds = win.getBounds()
+     const work = screen.getDisplayNearestPoint(screen.getCursorScreenPoint()).workArea
+     win.setBounds({
+       ...bounds,
+       x: Math.round(work.x + work.width / 2 - bounds.width / 2),
+       y: Math.round(work.y + work.height - bounds.height - LIFT)
+     })
+   }
+ 
+   private window(): BrowserWindow {
+     if (this.win) return this.win
+     const win = new BrowserWindow(
+       createScribeOptions(process.platform, this.page.preload, { width: WIDTH, height: HEIGHT })
+     )
+     // Above a full screen app and on whichever space is in front. Never this
+     // call without `skipTransformProcessType`: it turns the app into an
+     // accessory on macOS and the icon leaves the dock for good.
+     win.setAlwaysOnTop(true, 'screen-saver')
+     win.setVisibleOnAllWorkspaces(true, {
+       visibleOnFullScreen: true,
+       skipTransformProcessType: true
+     })
+     win.excludedFromShownWindowsMenu = true
+     win.on('closed', () => {
+       this.win = null
+     })
+     win.webContents.once('did-finish-load', () => {
+       if (this.settings) win.webContents.send('scribe:settings', this.settings)
+     })
+     if (this.page.devUrl) void win.loadURL(`${this.page.devUrl}#scribe`)
+     else void win.loadFile(this.page.file, { hash: 'scribe' })
+     this.win = win
+     return win
+   }
+ }
