Looking at the 48px scale, L2, L3, L4, and L6 all read convincingly as a nib touching a line—like a pen mid-stroke. The nib shape is clear with its flat top, taper, and vent hole sitting on the written line. At 16px they compress into a wedge-on-bar shape that stays clean and readable. L3 with its small gap stands out as the strongest option at 48px, where the nib and line remain visually distinct without any muddiness.

Comparing L1 against L3: L1 is a clean wedge with a dot at 16px, but it doesn't communicate writing. L3 actually conveys the act of writing. The real problem emerges at smaller sizes—L2 through L6 all start reading like a trophy or wine glass on a pedestal rather than a pen on paper, because the symmetric wedge sitting above a centered line creates that stand-like silhouette. The fix would be to offset the line so it's not centered under the nib, breaking that symmetrical trophy reading.

I'm exploring positioning the nib at one end of the line instead. For left-to-right writing, the pen should logically sit at the right end where it's actively writing, with the line trailing to the left. I'm testing a tilted nib (around 15-20°) leaning into the line's right end, though I'm worried a slight tilt on a symmetric wedge might just look accidental rather than intentional.

Looking back at the L-row design, the "nib over the line" version genuinely reads as a fountain pen above writing, which works well. I want to push further though by breaking the symmetry — trying variations like an upright nib with the line offset left, a tilted nib with a full-width line, or an upright nib paired with a wavy line instead of straight.

M4 with a gentle wave under the nib feels most promising since it reads as actual handwriting rather than a pedestal, though at 16px the amplitude might be too subtle to survive. M3 with a 15° tilt is stronger — the lean clearly signals "a pen in hand" and breaks away from the pedestal feel entirely, distinct from a pencil's steeper angle. I'm working out the geometry for a tilted nib version now, rotating around the nib's center while keeping the overall mark centered in the box. Now I'm working through the rotation matrix calculations with the specific angle values, transforming each corner point of the nib relative to the tip to see where they end up after the 16° rotation. The bounding box math is getting complicated with all the shifting and centering adjustments, so I'm going to skip the precise calculations and just hand-author a leaning nib instead, then verify it against the audit metrics afterward.

A cleaner approach: position the nib tip at the right end of the baseline so the line represents the actual writing stroke and the nib sits at the writing edge — that's unambiguous. I'm aiming for roughly an 18° rightward lean with the tip around (13.5, 18.8), working out the top edge coordinates by projecting the nib axis upward at that angle.

The geometry is tight though — a tilted nib wedge needs more horizontal space than the box allows. I'm testing different dimensions: reducing the nib length and half-width to keep everything within bounds, currently trying length 13 with half-width 4.2 to see if the corners stay inside the 21.75 limit.

The core tension is that a tilted nib has to be small to fit, and small means it becomes illegible mush. So I'm back to the real choice: either ship the upright nib sitting on a written line, or just the nib mark alone. The deciding factor is legibility at 16 pixels — whatever I pick needs to be clearly distinguishable from every other mark already in the set.

The nib alone is unmistakably different from the warning glyph, which is a squat upward-pointing triangle with a bar and dot, whereas the nib is a tall downward-pointing wedge with a single dot positioned high. The nib with a line underneath it is equally distinct from everything else and actually communicates "writing" more directly, though there's a risk it reads as a trophy or stamp instead. Both are clean at 16 pixels, but the nib-on-line version carries more information while staying crisp.

I'm leaning toward the nib-on-line design because the line is what differentiates it from just a pointed object and helps distinguish Scribe from Voice on the adjacent tile. The skill's own examples reinforce this approach with elements like the hill running off the frame and the page's fold. To address the trophy concern, I could extend the line edge to edge so it reads as a page rule rather than a base plate—a rule runs off both sides while a base would be narrower than or equal to the object itself.

Let me work through the proportions: if I widen the line to 18.5, the box becomes roughly 18.5 by 18.2, giving a geometric mean of about 18.35 versus the target 17—that's a 7.9% overage, just inside the 8% threshold and capped so it passes. But now the nib at 11.9 wide against an 18.5-wide line reads more like a wide mark than a writing implement, so I should probably adjust the nib proportions too to keep the visual balance.

Let me test a final configuration with a slightly wider nib at 13 against a 17-wide line, keeping the other elements consistent, and then run the comparison to see which pair works best.
The nib-on-a-line reads. Let me settle the proportions.

But I realize most of that second group is chrome that should already be non-selectable, so the real challenge is isolating the actual content areas. ## How to test it

Ask a thread agent for work that divides, and say the parts out loud. It only sends one out if the shape of the ask makes that obvious:

> Send a helper to list every test suite under `tests/` that touches the music panel, and while it does that, tell me what `src/shared/games.ts` holds.

What you should see, in order: a line from the agent saying who it sent where, a chip under it with a generated mark and the helper's name, the chip reporting its own latest step while it works, and the answer arriving back in the middle of the parent's turn. Click the chip and the helper opens in the side panel as an ordinary thread, with its steps, its diffs, its files, and a composer at the foot that steers just that agent.

Two things about who is on the thread. The mid-turn arrival only reads that way on Claude, which is the one CLI that takes a steer. On Codex, Kimi or Grok the answer is queued and starts the moment the current turn ends. And the host has your restart in it now, so a spawn coming back 404 is no longer the first thing to check.

If you want the wiring proven without spending a model on it: `yarn test tests/subagents.integration.test.ts`.

## When one spawns

There is no trigger. The agent is handed a curl line and a paragraph about dividing work, and it decides. That is the whole of it, which is why the preamble is worded the way it is: send out the parts that can happen at the same time, keep one for yourself, and do not send out work that sits on the files you are holding.

The preamble is only written into the prompt when there is room for at least one more, so an agent with its hands full is not told about a thing it cannot do.

## When one never does

- **Helpers off in Settings.** Yours alone, kept in that window, said again on every connect. Off means your agents never send work out **and never take anybody else's**, because it is your tokens and your files.
- **The machine it would land on has them off.** A named provider whose owner has said no is refused rather than quietly run somewhere else.
- **A named provider nobody here is running.** Refused, not fallen back to the parent's own, or the request reads as ignored.
- **A `/btw` aside.** A question on the side answers itself.
- **Two levels down.** A helper may send one out, a helper's helper may not, and the brief tells the first one not to unless the task says so.
- **A stale promptId.** Every route names the run asking, and the host takes it only while that run is one it has going right now. That is what keeps a helper reachable from the thread that sent it and nowhere else.
- **A helper somebody stopped** wakes nobody. Its work was called off.

## The numbers

Four at once per machine by default, which is the count on the Helpers page, up to 20. Eighty helpers over the life of one thread. Forty wakes, after which they still run and still report on their chips but stop interrupting. Returns inside 1.5s of each other arrive as one interruption. `/agents/wait` is capped at 60 seconds and the preamble says to prefer working over waiting.

The one thing none of this covers is two agents editing the same file at the same time. Half of that is words in the brief and the other half is the panel listing what each helper changed, so a clash is something you see rather than something you find later in a diff.
